summary: For 7–8 year olds, build the contact vs non-contact force distinction from first-hand experience. A force is a push or pull arising from an interaction between two objects. Contact forces (pushes and pulls made by touching, such as a hand pushing a door, plus friction, air resistance and upthrust) act only when objects touch; non-contact forces (magnetism, gravity, static electricity) act across a gap. Magnetism is the most child-manageable tactile example of action at a distance. The central hurdle is children expecting a force to need contact ('how can the Earth pull a ball it isn't touching?'); treat action-at-a-distance as genuinely remarkable, not obvious. Keep magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic forces separate while noting they share 'act at a distance' behaviour. At this age avoid newton-meters, field language and iron filings.
misconceptions: Forces must require contact — non-contact action feels impossible ('how can the Earth pull a ball it isn't touching?'); this is the core hurdle

Gravity is caused by magnetism / the Earth is a giant magnet — both act at a distance and are felt at the surface, so children conflate them. Discriminators: gravity ALWAYS attracts and acts on anything with mass; magnetism attracts AND repels and acts only on specific materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt)
Non-contact forces 'need air' to travel through — that magnets or gravity would stop working in a vacuum (false; no medium is required)
All metals are magnetic (transfer of 'metal = special' from electricity work)
A force is a property an object 'has' rather than an interaction between two objects

activities.title: Feel and see the pull across an empty gap
steps: Hold a real magnet and a paperclip in your hands and slowly bring them together until you feel the pull before they touch — describe the pull in your own words.

On a drag-and-release scene, move a magnet slowly toward a paperclip across an empty gap and watch a pull-arrow appear on the paperclip, pointing toward the magnet, before they touch, thickening as the gap narrows.
Repeat the same drag with two wooden blocks and notice that NO arrow appears until the blocks actually meet.
Say aloud which force reached across the empty space and which only acted on contact, and name a real-world parallel (the Earth pulling a dropped ball).
Toggle a 'remove the air' control and observe that the magnet's pull is unchanged.
activities.insight: Some forces (magnetism, and the Earth pulling a ball) act across empty space, while contact forces only act when two objects touch; the pull does not need air in the gap to work.

activities.title: Predict-then-test: what gets through the gap?
steps: Set a paperclip a small gap from a magnet and predict whether the pull still works when you slip a sheet of paper into the gap, and explain WHY.
Test it, then predict and test again with a steel baking tray slipped into the gap.
Discuss afterwards: did paper stop the pull? What did the steel tray do? What does that tell you about what the force needs to travel through and what materials it acts on?
Predict what would happen if the magnet and paperclip sat in a jar with all the air sucked out.
activities.insight: A non-contact force acts across a genuine gap and does not require air as a go-between; the magnet acts only on specific magnetic materials (such as iron, most steels, nickel and cobalt), which is why a magnetic steel tray interacts with the magnet while non-magnetic paper does not.

activities.title: Distinguish gravity from magnetism
steps: Compare: does the magnet pull an aluminium can the way it pulls a steel paperclip? Try it and say why the difference matters.
State one way gravity and magnetism are alike (for example, both act across a distance without the objects touching) and two ways they differ.
Decide, for a worked example, whether gravity or magnetism is acting: a dropped ball; a magnet picking up a steel pin; a magnet pushing away another magnet.
activities.insight: Gravity and magnetism both act at a distance but are different forces: gravity ALWAYS attracts and acts on anything with mass; magnetism attracts AND repels (repelling happens between two magnets) and acts only on specific materials (such as iron, most steels, nickel and cobalt).

activities.title: Sort everyday forces and explain the rule
steps: Drag or place each everyday force (a hand pushing a door, a hand pulling a rope, friction, air resistance, upthrust, magnetism, gravity) into a contact or non-contact category.
After each placement, state the test you used: 'do the two objects have to be touching?'
For a non-contact example, explain in a sentence that the force acts across a gap with no medium needed — do not just name the category.
Answer a short check: would a magnet still pull a paperclip in a vacuum? Why?
activities.insight: The dividing rule is whether the two objects must touch for the force to act; sorting correctly plus explaining the gap-spanning behaviour shows the concept, not just memorised labels.

checkQuestion: A magnet pulls a paperclip toward it across a small gap, without ever touching it. How can the magnet pull the paperclip when nothing is touching it?
checkAnswer: Magnetism is a non-contact force — it acts across a distance, so the magnet and paperclip don't need to touch. This is unlike a push, a pull by hand, or friction, which are contact forces that only work when the objects touch.
